draft.title: Scale
card: Scale is the size of the area a geographer looks at. Four common scales are local, regional, national and global.
local is a small area, such as a suburb or a creek. Regional is a larger area made of many localities, such as a river catchment or the Hunter Valley.
national is a whole country, such as Australia. Global is the whole Earth, or issues that cross many countries.
The same issue can look different at each scale. An explanation that fits at one scale may not fit at another, so geographers often check more than one.
draft.remember: Look at an issue at more than one scale, because what you find can change with the scale.

a.q: Which study of rainfall is set at a regional scale?
opts: Rainfall across the Murray-Darling Basin over a decade
Rainfall in one school's playground after a storm
Rainfall averages for Australia as one country
Rainfall patterns for every continent on Earth
a.why: A river basin is a large area made of many localities, so it is regional. A playground is local, a whole country is national and every continent is global.
a.clue: Think of an area bigger than a suburb but smaller than a country.

b.q: Dana finds that her town's average temperature has stayed steady for 20 years. A national study shows Australia warming over that time. What does this best show about scale?
opts: Findings at one scale may differ from those at another
One of the two studies must have made an error
The local result proves the national result is false
The national result must hold in every town
b.why: An explanation or pattern at one scale may differ at another, so a steady town and a warming country can both be correct. The tempting answer that one study is wrong assumes the scales must agree, which the card says is not so.
b.clue: Both results could be true at their own scale.

a.best: Rainfall across the Murray-Darling Basin over a decade

b.best: Findings at one scale may differ from those at another

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('may differ'), while every distractor uses an absolute word ('must', 'proves', 'must'). A test-wise student could pick it without knowing the idea.
